topics.topic: Authoritative time semantics, persisted representation, precision, and clock-sampling rules
questions: What authority supplies every instant written for the original function execution, the stop, and the recovery execution?
What does the trace's time field contain, and in what representation and precision is each instant stored and compared?
How many clock readings does one function execution take, and are the recorded start and end separate readings or one shared instant?
What clock supplies the original execution and recovery-replay instants, what each instant means, what representation is stored, and how many clock readings each execution takes?

What is the authoritative source and meaning of every instant written or compared, including instants written by a recovered execution, and what formal invariant and Required tests item demonstrate that rule?
In what exact representation are persisted instants carried—type, timezone, precision, and serialization—and what formal invariant and Required tests item demonstrate canonical representation?
Does this operation take one clock reading and use it for both start and end, or take separate readings, and how many readings does every other mutating operation take?

quotes:
- **Time** is `KernelInstant` (`epoch_us`, integer microseconds since the Unix
  epoch, UTC), the one representation of every recorded `*_at` field;
  `clock.kernel_now` returns it. `clock.monotonic_ns` returns one raw host
  monotonic reading in nanoseconds (`int`); a bounded wait derives its deadline
  from it and keeps it in memory only, never stored (A19 rule 2; decision 26).

execute_function_element: [ORCHESTRATION] MUST read the pinned implementation of the node with read_implementation, read every input's bytes with read_value_bytes into PortPayloads by port, take started_at from kernel_now, and call execute_function with the code, the payloads, the contract version's input and output ports and its resource_bounds; it writes no record and returns the outcome for its caller to write.

execute_function_element: [RETURN_SHAPE] Returns FunctionElementOutcome with the NodeExecutionDraft, whose ended_at is taken when the outcome is built, and the StoredValues and SpooledFiles of its outputs, each of the class highest_disclosure_class gives for the classes of every input value and file the element received — an input file list counting with its SpooledFilesRef's disclosure_class, even when empty — and each output SpooledFilesRef with that same class, so no output is of a lower class than an input.
judgement.why: The later contracts define the canonical instant representation and separately sampled start and end instants for original and recovered function executions, while State 2 already supplies the clock-source invariant and Required tests.

topics.topic: Boundary and enforcement of the requirement that replay has no effect
questions: Does “no effect” mean only that a function performs no Cabinet service effect, that it has no externally observable side effect of any kind, or that replay must also leave no additional internal artifacts such as logs, metrics, spooled bytes, or unnamed values?
What counts as an “effect” here: only externally applied service effects, or every durable mutation including output publication, spool writes and trace writes?
What observable actions are excluded by “has no effect,” and is this guaranteed by the function contract, enforced by the sandbox, or merely assumed when recovery re-executes it?

quotes:
A function node runs one admitted implementation of one contract: declared input
in, declared output out, no network, no filesystem beyond its input, no secret, no
service handle. The standard library's own entry points for the clock and for
randomness raise in a function, so it cannot depend on the time or on chance by
accident; code written to get time or chance some other way is not detected and is
judged by its outputs like any other. Every promise in these documents that a function
repeats itself — equal outputs on equal inputs, a repaired slot staying repaired, a
verdict that holds — is a promise about code whose outputs depend only on its inputs;
the kernel neither checks that nor masks any other fact of the process. An operation node invokes one declared
operation of one microservice; only the kernel performs it. An effect is never
hidden in code.

An element that does not
      succeed keeps no output: its NodeExecution names none, a value it produced
   is not stored, and the files its attempt spooled are discarded: no
   SpooledFile record names them and nothing reads them. Their bytes are
   removed at once only by a spool-ceiling refusal (A15 rule 3); after any
   other failure they stay in the run's spool, counted toward
   `spool_run_bytes_max`, until that spool is removed (A18 rule 4) or a later
   write to the same position replaces them — a position being the run, node,
   `map_index`, attempt number, port and list index, which only a retry of
   the same attempt number writes again, after a restart left that attempt
   without a record. Value bytes it published stay in the content-addressed area
   unnamed, reused by equal bytes until the next start removes them (A18 rule
   4); nothing reads either.
judgement.why: Purity means the function has no service effect and is isolated from network and host storage, but the kernel explicitly does not mask every process fact and permits unnamed kernel-managed output bytes to remain until replacement or cleanup.

topics.topic: How recovery reuses an attempt-numbered spool position when an unrecorded execution takes no attempt number
questions: How can recovery write the same attempt-numbered spool position when the carried rule says an execution that leaves no stored NodeExecution takes no attempt number?
How can recovery write the same attempt-numbered spool position when the received obligation says that an execution leaving no NodeExecution takes no attempt number?

How can recovery reuse the same attempt number when the received obligation says an execution that leaves no record takes no number; is a provisional number allocated before persistence, or must unrecorded artifacts use an unnumbered temporary position?

quotes: record_change: [DETERMINISM_OR_ORDERING] attempt_number of a NodeExecution written by RecordRunProgressChange, RecordReadOutcomeChange, RecordOperationFailureChange or DecideApprovalChange, and of an EffectAttempt written by RecordAttemptInFlightChange, is one more than the number of NodeExecutions the element already has, the length of list_node_execution_rows_by_element for its ElementKey, and RequestApprovalChange gives the EffectApproval it writes that same next number as its attempt_number without writing a NodeExecution; RecordRunProgressChange writes its executions in (node_id, map_index) order with an absent map_index before index 0. A NodeExecution whose files were spooled before it is written carries the attempt_number its caller spooled them under, the element's next number read as the count of its NodeExecutions plus one; the change is refused with RefusedError, writing nothing, when that number is no longer the element's next, and no caller ever chooses another number.

spool_file: [BEHAVIOR] When no SpooledFile record names file's position, MUST publish content with publish_spool_entry for the data_directory open_store opened and file, which replaces a file no record names left at that position by a change that failed. The attempt_number of file is the element's next number as the caller read it; spool_file assigns none.
judgement.why: The later store contract makes the number provisional for spooling by having the caller read the element's next record ordinal, reuse it on recovery while no record exists, and commit that same number with the eventual NodeExecution.

topics.topic: Store outcomes that count as refusing a NodeExecution record
questions: Exactly which store results count as refusing the record: only a definite rejection known not to have committed, or also timeouts, lost acknowledgements, transaction failures, and unknown commit outcomes?

Which store results count as having “refused” the record—only a definitive non-commit, or also a timeout, lost acknowledgement, uniqueness conflict, validation failure, or other outcome whose commit status is unknown?

quotes: record_change: [BEHAVIOR] MUST apply the one StoreChange given in one SQLite transaction that either writes every record the variant lists or nothing; it writes no record the variant does not list and trusts the caller for every decision of the caller's rule, checking only its own invariants: attempt numbers, unique and existing identities, existing linked records, and no edit of an immutable record. It checks no status of the record a lifecycle change updates and sets that change's fields whatever status the record has: the status a change may start from is the caller's rule, and one request ends before the next begins (A18), so no other request can have changed it meanwhile. A record of a kind the security-boundary note names never updated is only ever written once; a lifecycle change updates the fields its variant sets on the one record the change names, in place, and no other field of a written record ever changes.

record_change: [VALIDATION_ERROR] For RecordAttemptOutcomeChange and RecoverInFlightChange MUST raise RefusedError, writing nothing, when the named attempt's attempt_number is no longer one more than the number of NodeExecutions of its element; the concluding NodeExecution then takes that attempt's number. Any other broken invariant — a linked record missing, or an identity already present for a record that is written once — or a failed transaction raises StoreInternalError with nothing written.
judgement.why: The later store contract defines record changes as local atomic SQLite transactions and states that every refusal or failed transaction writes nothing, so an unknown committed-but-unacknowledged outcome is not an allowed store result.

topics.topic: Response and stop ordering after a function finishes but its trace record is refused
questions: What exactly does the surface return to the request whose function finished but whose trace record the store refused, and must that response be sent before the kernel stops?

judgement.why: P4 judged the same response-and-stop-ordering question on unchanged passages and found that the later module text requires an `internal_error` response before process termination.

precedent.topic: Response to the in-flight request before termination after its execution record cannot be stored
quotes:
It returns the stop to its caller, and
  `surface` ends the process: during a request after answering it as an
  internal error (A16 rule 7), during the start by stopping the start.
precedent.why: The module design decides that a request is answered as an internal error before the surface ends the process.

topics.topic: Whether mapped-node result-shape failures require an immutable node trace record
questions: Does the mapped-node failure caused by an oversized or over-deep delivered result list require an immutable node trace record under this rule, or may A13 rule 6 leave the failure represented only by element records and reader-side derivation?

quotes:
Every concluded attempt at an element, every skipped node and every
   `upstream_failed` node writes exactly one NodeExecution M23 — an owner's
   resolution of an unknown outcome writes none (A11). A mapped node's trace is
   its elements' records; it has a record of its own, without `map_index`, only
   when it ran no element: over an empty list (A13 rule 6), or when it was
   skipped or `upstream_failed` before any element.

a mapped node's value list above it fails the node for
   its dependants without changing any element's record (A13 rule 6)
judgement.why: State 2 defines mapped-node trace granularity explicitly: nonempty mapped nodes use their elements' records, and an oversized derived list changes no element record and creates no aggregate failure record.

topics.topic: Whether record commit is required for a completed function body to count as an execution
questions: If the function body returns but the process stops before attempting or completing the record write for a reason other than an explicit store refusal, was there a node execution that must have a record, or is record commit part of what makes it an execution?

quotes:
An execution completes only after every process of the environment is reaped
   and the exchange directory is removed. If that cannot be confirmed the output
   is discarded, the execution is recorded `crashed` with detail
   `cleanup_failed`, and the kernel process stops; runs it left `running` are
   recovered on the next start (A14 rule 5). If that record cannot be stored,
   the kernel process stops all the same, and recovery executes the element
   again, as it does every function element without a concluded record.

On start, before the surface accepts a request, the kernel turns every
   `in_flight` EffectAttempt into `unknown` (A11 rule 4) and then derives every
   run that has not ended — `running`, `awaiting_approval` or `pending` — again
   from its records, oldest first in store order, rewriting a stored status or
   waiting point that lags them (a decided approval, a resolved attempt, an
   outcome whose run change was lost), and advances, as the
   kernel actor, every run that derivation leaves `running`: a
   function element without a
   concluded record is executed again, which is safe because it has no effect; a `read`
   element without one is sent again; an operation element of another class with
   neither a concluded record nor an EffectAttempt was never sent and is advanced
   as if reached for the first time — an approved, unused approval covers it
   only while the rebuilt request has its `request_digest` (A10 rules 1 and 7).
judgement.why: Completion is defined by sandbox cleanup rather than record commit, and every function element lacking a concluded record is executed again after restart regardless of why the record is absent.
